questions.title: How does the butterfly factor $\bm{B}^F(k)$ actually get parameterized for training?
questions.question_body: In the paper, Equation 1 defines the butterfly factor $\bm{B}^F(k)$ as a matrix composed of four diagonal matrices $\text{diag}(\bm{d}_1)$ through $\text{diag}(\bm{d}_4)$. While the paper states these are 'some vectors', it doesn't explicitly say how these vectors are learned or if they are constrained in any way other than the block-wise rotation. Could someone clarify what the actual trainable parameters are within this specific component?

questions.title: Why does multiplying by an orthogonal matrix $\bm{R}$ preserve the 'pairwise angles' between neurons?
questions.question_body: The paper mentions that the core principle of Orthogonal Finetuning (OFT) is preserving the relational information of weight matrices, specifically the pairwise angles between neurons. I understand that an orthogonal matrix $\bm{R}$ satisfies $\bm{R}^\top\bm{R} = \bm{I}$. Can someone explain the linear algebra behind why this property ensures that the angles between the vectors in the weight matrix remain unchanged after the transformation $\bm{R}\bm{W}^0$?

questions.title: If BOFT involves a product of $m$ matrices, why is there no additional inference latency?
questions.question_body: I am a bit confused about the efficiency claim. The paper states that BOFT has no additional inference latency, but it also mentions that the orthogonal matrix $\bm{R}(m,b)$ is composed of a product of multiple butterfly components $\prod_{i=1}^m \tilde{\bm{B}}^b_{(d,i)}$. If we have to perform $m$ matrix multiplications during the forward pass at inference time, wouldn't that add latency compared to the original model? Or is there a way to 'collapse' these matrices first?

questions.title: How does the 'minimum free edges' desideratum interact with the orthogonality constraint?
questions.question_body: In Section 3, the authors describe an information transmission framework where they want to achieve 'minimum free edges' while maintaining 'dense connectivity.' However, they also mention that 'orthogonality injects a delicate constraint to the edges.' I'm struggling to understand this: if we are trying to minimize the number of edges to save parameters, but orthogonality forces certain edges to exist (or forces others to be zero), how does the authors' framework actually 'find' the optimal sparsity pattern? Is it a search problem or a structural construction?

questions.title: Why is a block-diagonal structure incapable of generating a dense matrix $\bm{R}$ in the information transmission view?
questions.question_body: The paper argues that BOFT is more expressive than the block-diagonal structure used in the original OFT because it can generate a dense matrix. Using the information transmission view (the grid-structured graph), can someone explain why a block-diagonal structure fails the 'dense connectivity' requirement? I'm trying to visualize the paths from the first level to the last level nodes.

questions.title: How does 'Multiplicative Dropout' differ from standard Dropout in the context of BOFT?
questions.question_body: I understand that standard Dropout (zeroing out elements) doesn't work for BOFT because it's a multiplicative weight update. The paper proposes 'Multiplicative Dropout' which replaces blocks with identity matrices. Does this mean the 'dropped' components effectively do nothing to the weight matrix? And how does this maintain the orthogonality of the total matrix $\bm{R}$ throughout the training process?
